rv.q: The music is given real punch by David White’s flamenco guitar-driven but otherwise stringless 30-piece orchestra.

So, despite the starry casting of this really patchy production – it is odd watching Kelsey Grammer and Nicholas Lyndhurst side by side, two sitcom legends from opposite sides of the Atlantic – what sustains most interest is simply the curiosity factor.
This creaking, effortful production, mounted in collaboration with English National Opera, doesn’t help.

Here all the stops are pulled out but, despite the commitment of the ENO orchestra, the result is a misfire. It says much that only a giant staircase, constantly lowered in James Noone’s metallic design, was moving.
The overall mise-en-scène is several Pythons short of the full Gilliam.

Producers Michael Linnit and Michael Grade don’t make a convincing case for reviving it: a mismatched celebrity cast and a by-numbers production mean that contemporary relevance, like chivalry, really is an impossible dream.
The luck runs out, however, with this revival of a long-neglected musical from 1965 based on Cervantes’ Don Quixote.
Some of its directorial choices are contradictory and superfluous but overall Man of La Mancha is really good fun.
But, overall, this is really only one for the musical theatre completists.
A long patch of similar sounding, slow-tempo and underwhelming songs compounded my disinterest and I began to yearn for it all to be over.
A lumbering show has its moments of familiarity as "The Impossible Dream" pops up again (and again), but mostly the dream that's impossible is to make it feel alive and relevant today.
It can now return to the museum.
As shows go, this has to be one of the most tragically dated and difficult to stage that London currently boasts.

cn.t: Critics largely dismiss this rarely-seen 1965 musical as a dated curiosity that deserved its obscurity, with Kelsey Grammer's miscasting and a charmless production failing to justify its West End return after 50 years.
